opus-5.5.text:
It's a really appealing idea, and I understand why people are drawn to it. The pitch is elegant: you take raw sensor data in, you get controls out, and you let a big model learn everything in between from data. No hand-designed interfaces, no brittle hand-off points between perception, prediction, and planning where information gets lost. And we've seen in other domains, language especially, that scaling a single large model on lots of data can produce remarkable capabilities. So the intuition that driving could work the same way is reasonable.

That said, when you think about what it takes to actually deploy a fully autonomous system, with no human behind the wheel, the picture gets more nuanced. A few things stand out to me.

First, the bar for safety is extremely high, and the failure modes you care about are rare. A pure sensors-to-controls model learned mostly by imitation will do very well on the common cases, but the long tail is where the hard work is. You need ways to understand why the system did something, to diagnose it, and to fix it without breaking ten other things. A monolithic black box makes that harder.

Second, validation. To ship a driverless product you need to convince yourself, and regulators and the public, that the system is safe. That's much easier when you have meaningful intermediate representations, like objects, their predicted futures, the road structure, that you can inspect, measure, and simulate against. Those structured outputs also make closed-loop simulation far more tractable, because you can reason about agents and scenarios rather than only re-rendering raw sensor data.

Third, the learning signal. Controls are a very sparse, low-dimensional supervision signal compared to the richness of the scene. Intermediate tasks like detection, tracking, and behavior prediction give you a lot of extra supervision that helps the model learn good representations efficiently.

So my view is that the right answer isn't really "modular versus end-to-end" as a binary. The trend, which we've embraced, is toward large models that are trained end-to-end in the sense that gradients and information flow across the whole stack, but that still keep structured, interpretable intermediate outputs. You get many of the benefits of end-to-end learning, less information loss and joint optimization, while retaining the ability to inspect, validate, and inject inductive bias and constraints where safety demands it.

And frankly, end-to-end models are very useful pieces of the toolkit even if they're not the whole driver. They're great for research, for learning priors, for powering simulation agents, and as components inside a larger system. I think the field will keep moving toward bigger, more unified models, foundation-model style, but for full autonomy at scale, you still want structure and the ability to verify. The question is less whether to go end-to-end and more how to get the benefits of scale while keeping the system safe, understandable, and improvable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here.

So the appeal is obvious, right? If you look at what's happened in computer vision, in language, in speech, the story over and over has been that a model trained end to end on enough data, with enough capacity, tends to beat a pipeline of hand-engineered components. The components were really our priors about how the problem decomposes, and it turns out the data often knows better. So the natural thought is, why not do the same thing for driving? Pixels and lidar points in, steering and acceleration out, let the gradient figure out the rest. It's elegant, it's conceptually simple, and it removes a lot of interface decisions that engineers otherwise have to make and argue about.

And I want to be clear that I think there's real substance behind that appeal. Where I've been at Waymo for many years, we've been moving in that direction continuously. Perception and prediction used to be very separate, and now they are much more tightly integrated. Behavior models are learned. A lot of the hand-coded logic has been replaced over time with learned components, and that trend is only going to continue. So the question for me is not learned versus not learned. That debate is over. The question is about what the decomposition looks like, what the interfaces are, and what the training signal is.

And that's where I'd push back a bit on the purest version of the story. A few things.

First, driving is a safety-critical, long-tail problem. A monolithic model that goes from sensors directly to controls is very hard to interrogate. When something goes wrong, you'd like to be able to ask, did it see the pedestrian? Did it predict they would step out? Did it decide to yield and then execute badly? If all you have is a control output, you have one very weak bit of signal, and you lose a lot of the ability to diagnose, to target data collection, and to validate. Intermediate representations, even if they are learned and even if they are not strictly human-interpretable, give you a lot of leverage there. They let you test components, they let you inject scenarios, and they let you build structured simulation. I actually think the simulation and evaluation story is the part people underestimate the most. The hard part of autonomy was never the median case, it's proving you handle the rare ones, and an end-to-end black box makes that proof harder, not easier.

Second, the supervision problem. Imitation learning from human driving gets you a long way, and it's a wonderful starting point, but human driving logs are mostly uneventful. The events you care about are rare and sometimes you don't want to imitate the human at all. So you need some way to reason about counterfactuals, to get signal from interventions, from simulation, from closed-loop evaluation. And once you're doing that, you are, almost by necessity, introducing structure. You need to know what the other agents are and where they are to perturb them in simulation. So the structure sneaks back in through the training setup, even if the deployed network looks monolithic.

Third, I'd say a lot of what gets called end-to-end in the field today is really end-to-end differentiable, or end-to-end trainable, rather than end-to-end unstructured. There's a big difference between those. You can have a system that has a perception stage, a behavior stage, and a planning stage, where gradients flow through all of them and where the interfaces are learned latents rather than hand-designed boxes, and that is end-to-end in the sense that matters. I think that is where the field is converging, and that is a lot more viable than the picture of one giant policy network with no internal structure at all.

And then there's a practical point, which is that foundation models have changed the conversation. Large vision-language models bring in world knowledge that you cannot get from driving logs alone. They know what a construction worker holding a stop sign means, they can read a hand-written detour sign. Bringing that in is enormously valuable, but you have to be thoughtful about how you combine a model that is slow and knowledgeable with a system that needs to make decisions at high frequency with hard latency and safety requirements. Again, that pushes you toward a layered architecture rather than a single uniform model.

So if I were to summarize, the appeal is real and the direction is right. More learning, fewer hand-engineered boundaries, more joint optimization. But I think the viable version of that for actually deploying a fully autonomous service, without a human to catch mistakes, is one that keeps enough structure to be testable, to be simulatable, and to be improved in a targeted way. The demos of a single sensors-to-controls network are genuinely impressive, and they're a great way to show how far learning can go. Getting from an impressive demo to a system that drives millions of miles without a driver is a different problem, and the structure you keep is a big part of what gets you across that gap.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is very clear. Ultimately, you want to optimize the system for driving well, and an end-to-end model gives you a way to learn directly toward that objective. You also avoid some of the constraints that come from designing interfaces between perception, prediction, and planning, where you may throw away information that would be useful downstream.

But there’s a big difference between demonstrating that a model can drive in a range of situations and establishing that it’s reliable enough for fully autonomous operation. The difficult questions are about rare situations, how you measure performance, and how you understand and fix failures. If the vehicle does something wrong, is it because it didn’t perceive something, because it misunderstood what another road user would do, or because it chose the wrong action? You still need ways to answer those questions, even if you train the system jointly.

So I wouldn’t frame this as a choice between learning and engineering structure. You can have a system that is increasingly trained end to end while retaining intermediate representations and auxiliary objectives that help with supervision, debugging, and validation. To me, that’s a very compelling direction. The practical test is whether the approach delivers measurable improvements in safety and generalization, especially in the situations where data is scarce.

sol-6.1.text:
The appeal is very clear. Ultimately, you want to optimize the system for driving well, and training from sensor inputs all the way to controls gives you a way to optimize that objective jointly. If you build separate components, you have to define interfaces and intermediate objectives, and those choices can limit what the overall system can learn.

But there’s a big difference between demonstrating that a model can drive and showing that it can operate reliably without a human fallback. The difficult questions are around the rare situations: how you get enough training signal, how you evaluate behavior, and how you understand what went wrong when the system makes a mistake. A single model doesn’t make those problems disappear.

I also don’t think end-to-end learning necessarily means giving up structure. You can have intermediate representations, auxiliary tasks, and components with useful inductive biases while still training much of the system jointly. So I see a lot of value in moving toward more integrated learning. The practical question is which architecture lets you improve driving performance while also giving you the tools to validate it and establish confidence in its safety.
